Name: Jan M Savage
Question: As a beginner, what computer programming language should I learn first?
Answer: Opinions vary on this, and facts are not certain. The core of the matter is, language choice does matter, but most people, even the ‘experts’ think it does not. Matter for what? Well, given enough grit, you can learn programming in any language, and that has worked fine for a lot of people. The key point in my answer is: but why should one suffer when one can avoid the suffering? Programming is supposed to be enjoyable. Learning to program is hard, but it’s the good kind of hard, the kind utilized by video-game makers. So, it’s supposed to be mentally challenging in a fun way, but some language choices convince a learner that programming is anything but fun, and probably impossibly difficult to learn. The ideal programming language that should be used as one’s first, should be complex enough to teach real-world programming, but simple enough to not overwhelm the learner. It should be pleasant to write, easy to read, efficient (in every way), and immediately useful, so that the learner can also derive extrinsic motivation (say, for writing their own software and becoming a tech entrepreneur). It should be free (and open-sourced), but still backed by a solid organization or team, so that the learner doesn’t feel their effort would be wasted because the language dies or goes out of ‘fashion’. It should have a useful and large quantity of libraries so that the learner should avoid re-inventing the wheel (like in Scheme); by all means, learn how to re-invent the wheel once, for practice, but then have access to a package/gem/crate/library to avoid drudgery. It should have excellent docs, written with beginners in mind, and leaving nothing to ‘guesswork’ and Google. Currently, only Dart, Go, Ruby, Rust, and Cuis have docs that match this criteria. Python docs are horrid, by contrast. Good compiler messages are important as well, and in this only Rust and Dart shine. It should be high-level enough to enable the learner to deeply and truly learn algorithmic thinking and all the advanced programming/CS topics, while at the same time, ‘practical’ enough so that it’s not a mere ‘academic’ language. Haskell qualifies here, as do Scala, Rust, OCaml, but Haskell outshines them all in this aspect, but leans more towards being a language-research lab, that by the way, can also be used in practice. Rust goes the opposite way, with practical-first. Scala and F# hit a middle point. OCaml has changed a lot recently and is currently the number-one under-rated language in the world. So as you can see, it’s not easy to recommend just one language. But you must start with one language first. What to do? A bit of compromise is fine, at this stage, since there’s no other choice. And while we’re at it, there’s also the issue of functional and object-oriented paradigms (among the most popular, often-used ones, with OO being the more real-world, more popularly-used, while FP slowly encroaching). So, then the task becomes simpler. Some opine that one has to start with FP, while others suggest imperative/OOP first. Given that the industry runs on OOP mostly, and since it’s easier than FP, (and while I think FP is best in an ideal world), realistically speaking, the learner should start with OOP, and then move to FP, mimicking the industry trends. So the question becomes: which true OOP language fits the above list of criteria? You want true OOP (pure OOP, the kind where everything really is an object, and not a semi-OOP like Java, for instance). And you want a true OOP language that is simple and elegant enough without being academic or ‘toy’; powerful without being overwhelming, immediately useful, and a language that will serve the learner for years to come. It should have great docs and tooling, and should have survived the grayness of time and the caprice of fads. It should instantly cheer up the learner who will sneer at all the people who have no idea what they’re missing (and are unaware of it, too). Does such a language exist? Of course it does. It’s called Smalltalk. There are several dialects: Pharo is not for beginners, and Squeak is too much at once. The best dialect is Cuis. They even have a programming 101 book that teaches both programming and Cuis-Smalltalk (which is essentially the classic Smalltalk-80 with added improvements ‘stolen’ from Pharo and Squeak) in a fun way (you will be writing a game!). After you master Cuis-Smalltalk, lunge for FP and either start with Haskell or OCaml and after that, you’re set. For Haskell, Hudak’s *‘Haskell School of Expression’* is the best intro to FP I’ve ever seen. It assumes a programming 101 background which you will have gotten from the Cuis-Smalltalk book. While there, you should also keep learning more, as programming can’t be learned from one or two books. All the excellent old books teaching programming in Smalltalk-80 run on Cuis, and are 99% compatible. Some of the greatest OOP books have been written with Smalltalk-80 as the language of instruction. For FP, you will need to keep learning—the next book should be: Real World Haskell. After all this, you will know what books you will need.

Answer: It means: The language has a sound type system: i.e. you will never get into a state where an expression evaluates to a value that doesn't match the expression's static (the type you assigned originally) type. For instance, if an expression's static type is String, at runtime you are guaranteed to only get a string when you evaluate it. In the jargon, we call it: type system soundness. Languages like Java, C# and Dart all possess sound type systems, and the advantages are: So, it makes your programs: Let’s experience this. In such a language, when you assign a value to a variable, you’re also assigning a type. For instance, in Python you can totally do this: The first is a float type, and the second is an int type, but Python is like that frenemy who won’t tell you have something on your teeth; this can lead to very-hard-to-find bugs. On the contrary, in Dart, you can’t be so frivolous: Will not compile (the program won’t run). That’s because you promised num to be an int type, and then later you reneged on that promise by assigning to it a float value. What are you, some kinda cheater? Question: What are some ways that programming was better in the past?
Answer: Eh… It wasn’t. There was no internet, so if you got stuck, you had only access to books, or you had to figure it out yourself, or ask someone (if you could find!) who knew. When there was internet, there was no Stackoverflow, no Quora, etc. There weren’t that many cool programming languages. Programmers were stuck with a few choices, like a forced marriage to some semi-ugly, bad-mannered evil fairy… Now we have so many excellent languages that take advantage of (and were designed specifically for) the recent advances in hardware. Go and Swift are two examples. Also, the languages that were not that excellent, have been updated. C# has been aggressively updated, currently in version 14; PHP 8 is very good, Raku put an end to Perl’s bad rep, etc. etc. Even Java has ‘borrowed’ things from Haskell, and Haskell became production-ready. :) Computers were sucky. Now we have faster computers, better screen monitors, better keyboards. Writing advanced web applications was a nightmare. Now, although the choices have increased, the problems have decreased, so there’s less headache involved. You can write an app in Elixir without touching Javascript. Or in Blazor (C#) and use minimal Javascript, for instance. You can also avoid Js altogether via Purescript, both for back- and frontend. Even Javascript pulled its act together and improved a lot. You can efficiently generate HTML in languages that look and behave like Haskell. You have Htmx. You can also write the same Electron-based desktop app in Swift and make the program many times faster, smaller and safer. I could go on. But if we had to specifically fish for aspects that were distinctly better than today’s, I would say people were nicer and happier (possibly because people’s dopamine levels weren’t out of whack due to addictive online content), programmers were more qualified, food tasted better (and was safer); but these are peripheral aspects.

Question: Computer Science: Why is recursion more elegant than iteration?
Answer: Costya Perepelitsa's answer to Computer Science: Why is recursion more elegant than iteration? already does an excellent job. Another good answer is John Colagioia's answer to Computer Science: Why is recursion more elegant than iteration? In agreement with them, here are my two cents: Wiedenbeck (1989) reports (bold is mine): Experiment 1 showed that learning the iterative version of a mathematical function first did not facilitate learning the recursive version. A big part of success in Experiment 1 was attached to detecting the sequential nature of the computation. When a subject had correctly induced this in one kind of problem, either iterative or recursive, he or she was more easily and quickly able to apply the same idea in the other kind of problem in spite of its different format. Thus, subjects were helped most by learning a general type of solution to expect (a sequence), not by specifically having experience with iterative (or recursive) problems first. In the context of CS, recursion is fundamental to problem-solving in computer science independent of its role as a programming technique. For instance in graph theory, artificial intelligence, neural networks, logical programming, and recursive database querying. McCraken (1987) claims: Recursion is fundamental in computer science, whether understood as a mathematical concept, a programming technique, a way of expressing an algorithm, or a problem-solving approach . He continues: Is recursion an advanced topic? Absolutely not. And: It is too important and too valuable to be belittled by showing a recursive factorial function in CS1, which conveys almost nothing of its power. Question: How do I become a coder, and what basic knowledge do I need to learn?
Answer: You should aspire to become a programmer, not a ‘coder’ (there's no such thing as being a coder). Further, you can't become a programmer with ‘basic knowledge’. I don't blame you, of course. You may have had the erroneous idea that ‘coding is easy’ because some charlatan probably tried to hardsell you snakeoil (“become a coder in 2 weeks!”). Programming is a serious occupation, requiring the same dedication, attention to details, rigor and professionalism as medicine, law, astrophysics etc. Writing programs is not a matter of memorizing syntax and some computer science terms and concepts. In fact, correctly viewed, programming is the flip side of discrete mathematics. And even if you ignore this mathematical part, as an art, programming involves deep reasoning and a wide array of skills, a never-ending stream of ever-changing knowledge, and not finally, a combination of computer science and the finest outcomes of good decision-making. The result is experience, the kind a grandmaster of chess gains after battling it out the hard way. Nobody becomes a chess grandmaster without that sort of game-theoretic experience: knowledge of chess rules doesn't make one a proficient player. Programmers battle it out against complexity, bugs, the often clueless management, the asshole(s) on the team, lifelong education, etc. etc. Only after years of discovering truths and tricks no book teaches can you become a programmer. Since this is a chicken-and-egg problem, the best thing for you, at least now, is to solve a lot of programming exercises so as to practice problem-solving. At its heart, programming really is problem-solving.

Question: What is the purpose of using a programming language instead of machine language?
Answer: The same purpose or reason why you don’t wash your laundry with your hands but instead use a washing machine and a dryer. Programming languages are abstractions. Abstractions help us focus on what matters to us, without distorting the reality too much. A map is an abstraction of a geographic location. A map focuses on roads, building names, etc. instead of everything in a satellite image. This is why maps are useful: they provide us with enough information that can be useful for a particular purpose. Programming languages do the exact same thing: they provide tools at a level of abstraction that help us focus on using the computer to solve hard problems. Initially, imperative programming languages were abstractions over machine languages. The first most successful of these was C. Later, functional programming languages provided further abstractions away from the machine. The industry hasn’t caught up yet but because it can’t really. Too much legacy code has been written in object-oriented languages and it’s impossible to ignore such sunk costs.

Question: Why do so many programmers think that JavaScript is a bad programming language?
Answer: (In this answer, my focus is on the entrepreneurial programmer who is free to choose what language he wishes to program in. So, I won’t be commenting on the team/enterprise aspects). The same reason why programmer X thinks language Y is not as good as language X. Programmers are human (except Bob. He ‘identifies as’ a synth), and for humans, there’s a thing called the endowment effect. Investopedia summarizes: Do you see the logic now? Programmers programming in language X for n years will ‘place a higher value’ because they ‘own’ (expertise in) language X. If there’s another language as good as X, they’d value it less compared to X. Programmers build psychological identities for themselves: John says he’s a C++er, Lily will say she’s a Lisper. You see my profile? I’ve mentioned that I’m a Haskeller. This is the ‘symbolic significance’. The emotional one can be tested when you tell a programmer that X, his language of choice, is not as good as language Y which he doesn’t know (and doesn’t want to learn). You’ll meet with the most vehement of disagreements! But understandably so. A programmer who’s been making a living in language X is not going to admit the language he’s been using (and enjoying) is not as good as language Y, even if he is dimly aware that, upon investigation, it may be true. We grow to like the quirks of the languages we’re most familiar with, and then those quirks don’t bother us anymore because we can anticipate, ameliorate, or eliminate them. For instance, for Javascript, you were probably told that each of these lines won’t work: Actually, except line 10, they all do work and if you want to make line 10 work as well, you just add a semicolon to the end of line 7. Like so: (But it is recommended to use semicolons all the time as a matter of best practice). Thus, if you ask a Javascripter, he’ll probably give you plenty of reasons why Javascript is not so bad as they say it is; in fact, he may even show you how Javascript can do certain things better than most languages out there. By the same reasoning, some programmers may claim Javascript is not a good language because they don’t understand it well enough even if they are forced to work in it. Unless they popped their cherries on Javascript, they’ll always have biased opinions because one’s first language is like one’s first kiss, and they will have already been influenced by their first language. This is not to say all programmers are like this. A real, professional programmer holds no silly biases like this. Like enthusiastic stamp collectors, we collect languages and don’t become emotional about them. Each language is a unique tool; we use the right tool for the right job, and if new tools appear, we acquire them, warts and all. We don’t develop rosy pictures or dismal attitudes. We understand both the strengths and weaknesses of a given language, and use them in accordance with those conditions. In other words, we don’t care whether language X is better than language Y. This is how you tell whether someone is an amateur. The pros simply learn the language, and use it correctly. Will X be better than Y for a pro? Well, it’s not so easy as that. Better for what? Each language has its own scenarios. Of course, we may also have personal preferences: we might prefer Clojure over Scala, but these are subjective, and unexplainable (why is your favorite color blue? you won’t be able to explain that!). So, making generalized (and subjective) statements about languages is futile and incorrect. You may like C++, and I may not—but so what? There will be a class of problems only C++ can solve, but also a class of problems C++ would be a terrible choice for. It all depends.

Question: Why is coding not for everyone?
Answer: By coding, you mean programming. Because it’s hard. At the advanced levels, of course. But so too at the beginner level. In fact, at the beginner level, it’s harder on the novice, than it is at advanced levels on a pro. In other words, the difficulties are not of the same type. The beginner’s difficulty is overcome in major shifts in thinking types and tenacity levels—requiring deeply passionate reasons to sustain the change brought about with such shifts. The most important shift in thinking comes from leaving a passive observer status, and changing into an active problem-solver one. You already know that as we go to school, our intellectual responses are mostly passive, even in the case of homework and exams: we’re reactively trying to appease someone who has the ‘key’ to the solutions. This transfers to our general mental models in life: somebody else has all the solutions, and we must seek those solutions from them. This seeking is passive, because it transfers the responsibility of deciding what a solution is to someone else. Consequently, one psychological drawback of such a passive solution-seeking manifests itself in reduced and abnormal tenacity levels. People, generally then, tend to become a herd of shortcut-seekers looking for ready, black-and-white answers and solutions. In entering the world of programming, at once, you become aware that solution-seeking is your personal responsibility. The answers and solutions are on the other side of the problem and nobody but you must uncover or find them. Because most people operate on reduced tenacity levels (which was being addressed by Grinder and Bandler in their NLP books), however, it is quite difficult to attempt and keep adopting this active, independent problem-solving stance. Question: What's the use of async controller actions in C#/.NET?
Answer: —Jan, can you explain what initiating an asynchronous operation really means? Well, it means using a controller action in C#/.NET for operations that take an unacceptably long time to complete. —Such as? Things like querying a database, reading or writing files, making network requests, or doing complex calculations or data processing. —Why do I need to async such tasks? Well, if you don’t, in other words, if they’re done synchronously, you would cause the current thread to wait until they’re finished. —Is that bad? Bad is not the right word, although it can be. I’d say wasteful. —Ok, how does it work? An async operation is initiated that consists of two steps: a thread is used to initiate the task, but because the action takes time, the thread is freed for other tasks; once the initiated task is completed, a thread is re-employed to finish the remainder of the task. See a diagram here: —That is not very clear, although I get the main idea. Could you elaborate? Sure. Let’s see a more detailed one: When the await keyword is used, it says “start this operation, and then free up the current thread to do other work instead of waiting for this operation to finish”. —What’s an example of ‘this operation’? How is ‘this operation’ done now that we freed up the thread? Won’t it need a thread to be finished? An example is fetching data from the database. Now the responsibility of the task has been passed to the database to do its job, so our application thread is available again. We free the thread, so some other tasks can use it. —Ok, why is freeing up the current thread a good thing? Well, then the server can handle a higher number of concurrent requests without exhausting the available thread pool. Particularly important in scenarios with high traffic or long-running operations. —So, it allows my application to handle more requests and do other work while waiting for the database operation to complete? Exactly. It improves the overall responsiveness and scalability of your application. —Right. Can you give me a code example? Yeah, and await on 17 calling _context.Employees.ToListAsync(), a potentially long-running operation (because it queries a database). —Ok, so what does await do? It tells the .NET runtime to “pause” the Index() method and return control to its caller. Now the current thread is freed up to do other work. —And what happens after the database operation is completed? Once the database operation is complete, the .NET runtime schedules the remainder of the Index() method to continue executing. —Correct me if I’m wrong: when the operation is complete, the .NET runtime is notified to schedule the remainder of the async method (the code after the await keyword) to run on a thread from the available thread pool. Yes. But it doesn’t have to be the same thread that was started initially. It can be any thread. —Interesting. So in your code example, what is the remainder of the async method? Question: What are SOLID design principles?
Answer: This is a huge topic but we can break it down into three levels of analysis. Let’s start with what the letters stand for: Now let’s see what these phrases exactly mean. SRP A class should have one responsibility, and only one, reason to change. In a restaurant, each person has a specific role: the chef prepares the food, the server brings it to the customers, and the dishwasher cleans up. Each role has a single responsibility. So, this is bad (C#): But this is good because each class has a single responsibility: OCP Software entities (classes, modules, functions, etc.) should be open for extension but closed for modification (OCP). Consider a vending machine. It’s designed to dispense snacks and drinks without needing to be opened up. But if you want to add a new type of snack or drink, you can just fill one of the slots with it. This complies with OCP. Now suppose there’s a simple Kitchen class that prepares a Meal : This class violates OCP because whenever you add a new type of meal, you must modify the PrepareMeal method. How to refactor the above to comply with the OCP? Create an IMeal interface with a Prepare method. Each meal type should implement this interface. The Kitchen class then calls the Prepare method on any meal, without knowing its specific type: LSP Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types. Any kitchen appliance should be replaceable with another model as long as it fits the same space and fulfills the same function. This C# code is LSP-compliant: This one violates LSP: Why? Well, subclasses should be substitutable for their base classes without causing errors. If you replace an Oven object with a Microwave object, the program won’t work as you intended it. ISP In a kitchen, not every appliance has the same functions; a blender blends, an oven bakes. Each appliance offers only the functions that are relevant to its purpose. This below is ISP compliant because interfaces are specific to their use: DIP Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use. High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions. Abstractions should not depend on details. Details should depend on abstractions. (DIP) A chef should not depend on a specific farmer for ingredients but rather on a general supplier, allowing for flexibility in sourcing. This here below is DIP compliant since high-level modules do not depend on low-level modules: —— Let’s summarize Each building (class) has a single responsibility (SRP), like being a residential apartment or a commercial office. As the city grows, new buildings can be added (OCP) without modifying existing ones. Residential apartments can be substituted for each other (LSP) without affecting the functionality of the city. Buildings only provide the necessary services (ISP) that their residents require. The city's infrastructure (high-level modules) like roads and utilities depend on abstract plans (abstractions) rather than specific building details (DIP). Question: Can programming/coding be summed up to "the art of managing memory"?
Answer: Managing memory has always been a matter of necessity, not choice. Now that this problem has almost been solved (Rust) and since in most cases nowadays programmers need not manually manage memory, then we can summarize programming as: The art of creatively devising and deriving computable, efficient, elegant and safe solutions to various problems that need a programmatic solution. I say this last bit, because, obviously, you can’t use programming to solve every problem. For instance, much as I miss my late mom, I can’t bring her back using programming (or using any other methods). The other issue is that of safety, which is paramount and usually somewhat ignored. Let’s not digress into the reasons, but for now, it’s logically sufficient to claim that safe programs that don’t crash or behave unexpectedly are better and preferred over those that do cause problems. The human element is just as important. Elegant programs are readable and beautiful, and programmers should strive to write code that can be reasoned about, and ideally, proved to be correct and safe. Despite the fact that we have faster hardware now, writing efficient solutions is always preferred over inefficient ones. Finally, we can’t ignore the creativity dimension. At the end of the day, a program is a means to an end. That end has to be creatively dealt with. Not only in how the program solves the problem, but also in presentation and general feel. For a good example of this, see Halloy, written in Rust, a good example of a program that combines efficiency, safety, and a good user experience.

Question: What is the difference between functional programming and object-oriented programming? Is Python an OOP language?
Answer: This deserves a booklet—but I’ll give the basic difference: The first layer of programming paradigm is procedural, or imperative. It’s like a recipe for primitive level cooking: You get the idea. Now, in the previous case, you made use of a flat stone you found in the forest. And used a stick you found nearby to stir the food. And ate it on a leaf. OOP is an advanced imperative paradigm. Here now you develop a blueprint for creating utensils. You develop maps for making plates, bowls, ladles, knives etc. And you also make blueprints for creating mini-robots that you can direct (these are called objects, and the blueprint is the class that gives birth to these objects). In OOP, you do this: In OOP, you represented the things in the real world as virtual objects, but at its core, it’s still procedural: do this, then do that. Procedural paradigm fits exactly how a machine operates. The programmer does what the computer wants and understands. In FP, we go up one more layer of abstraction. Now imagine you’re like a master chef in a well-equipped kitchen. You have a variety of tools and ingredients at your disposal, but you follow a different philosophy; you don’t mutate ingredients: you transform them into something else such that the original ingredient remain the same (at least on the surface to make it pleasant and less error-prone for the programmer. At its heart though, FP still relies on the machine’s imperative methods but the programmer need not concern herself with this level of detail ). Here’s a tentative outline: In this kitchen, you don’t have robots (objects) that change their state. Instead, you have a collection of tools (functions) that you apply to your ingredients (data) to create new ingredients. The original ingredients are never altered; they are immutable. This is the essence of FP: data is immutable and functions are pure. They don’t cause side effects; they don’t change the state of the world. They just transform input into output. In FP, you do what makes sense from a mathematical and logical perspective. You’re not concerned with the low-level details of how the computer works. Instead, you’re focused on expressing your program in a declarative way: you specify what you want, not how to get it. This is a higher level of abstraction compared to procedural and OOP paradigms. It’s like cooking at a molecular gastronomy level, where you care about the transformations of the ingredients at a fundamental level, and the process of cooking becomes a scientific and artistic expression. This is the beauty of FP: it’s about transformations, not mutations. It’s about expressing what you want, not how to do it. It’s about thinking at a higher level of abstraction. It’s a different way of thinking about programming, just like molecular gastronomy is a different way of thinking about cooking. Finally, Python can be used in both OO and FP ways, but to some extent only. Python is primarily procedural, hence more OO than FP. A good FP language is Haskell—the best. A good, true OO language is Ruby.

Question: What are the disadvantages of recursive functions?
Answer: They can be slower than iterative loops—speaking plainly—and sometimes more difficult to write. However, this is only because of the wrong language choice. Recursion is tedious in Python (this function recursively checks whether parentheses are balanced or not): Look at all that cruft. It suffers from Indexitis (coined by P. Wadler) among other crufty verbiage. However, to be fair, the iterative Python version is somewhat simpler: In Haskell, recursion is faster and easier than iteration. Look at the same function in recursive Haskell: Because of Haskell’s so-called Just-when-needed philosophy, computation of a thing occurs only when it’s needed (aka Lazy evaluation). Haskell’s laziness ensures that recursion never runs into problems in 90% of the cases (its compiler will do all sorts of under-the-hood optimizations), and in the 10% of the cases, allows you to use tail call optimizations (TCO) to further prevent any problems. The other ‘perceived’ disadvantage is psychological. People have been scared into thinking recursion is a difficult concept, but this is always because the people who taught it didn’t really understand or know it. If you really want to learn recursion, read HDTP (beginners; otherwise Thinking Recursively with Java).

Question: Are IQ tests effective at measuring intelligence?
Answer: Take a look at this: A’s pattern is: B is: C is D is E is So what’s it going to be? If you think it’s D, this is what NNT says[1] about such choices: Real Life: In academia there is no difference between academia and the real world; in the real world there is. 1) When someone asks you a question in the real world, you focus first on “why is he/she asking me that?”, which shifts you to the environment (see Fat Tony vs Dr John in The Black Swan) and detracts you from the problem at hand. Philosophers have known about that problem forever. Only suckers don’t have that instinct. Further, take the sequence {1,2,3,4,x}. What should x be? Only someone who is clueless about induction would answer 5 as if it were the only answer (see Goodman’s problem in a philosophy textbook or ask your closest Fat Tony) [Note: We can also apply here Wittgenstein’s rule-following problem, which states that any of an infinite number of functions is compatible with any finite sequence. Source: Paul Bogossian]. Not only clueless, but obedient enough to want to think in a certain way. 2) Real life never never offers crisp questions with crisp answers (most questions don’t have answers; perhaps the worst problem with IQ is that it seem to selects for people who don’t like to say “there is no answer, don’t waste time, find something else”.)…. Intelligence has been touted as the ability to ‘pick patterns’. But the problem with such a definition is: sometimes, noise/chaos can present itself as patterns, due to randomness. For instance, a basketball hot hand, or a stock trader betting right for several years in a row. In other words, there may be no pattern at all, but it certainly looks like a pattern in the short run. What happens when the intelligence that was defined in terms of seeing patterns realizes, later, that the pattern was due to randomness, assuming there was a pattern in the first place? That brings us to the second issue. Who decides what pattern is there? Given various lines of reasoning, one could argue, almost reasonably, for a variety of patterns. In fact, this picture was most probably designed according to the original pattern by the person who designed the picture. But the problem is, the progression of patterns is not long enough to make any substantial claim about the validity of the pattern holding forever. This is known as the poor man’s induction, in mathematical circles. Further, there could be no pattern at all, and the designer is merely pranking people. All these issues point to the fact that IQ tests are just ‘intellectual garbage’ and nothing more. Truly highly-intelligent people have the ability to (among other abilities): As such, it’s impossible to measure intelligence in any scientific way; said another way, there are a multitude of ways we can do 1, 2 and 3. Worse, the same person will do 1, 2 and 3 with different frequencies and intensities given different temporal, contextual, and biological contexts. If you want to know who’s intelligent, your task becomes easier when you filter out all those who design, believe in, and participate in IQ tests as a measure of high intelligence. Question: Is there anything you don’t like about Functional Programming?
Answer: Structured programming was an improvement because it hid goto so that the programmers had access to higher-level, structured abstractions that they could easily reason about. SP is goto-less abstraction, but the goto is still there, hidden away. Functional programming is a similar improvement. Now, thanks to doing away with assignments, programmers have access to an even higher level of abstraction and the programs are even easier to reason about. FP is assignment-less abstraction over SP, the hardware still does the assignments, but these are no longer the programmer’s headache. FP encourages programming in the large, first coined by Deremer and Kron, in 1976. The higher level of abstraction available in FP empower the programmer to work in larger units than those found in non-FP languages (for instance, higher order functions allow more creative and programmatic freedom.). The most important, however, is taking advantage of parallelism. Especially now, since we have the hardware for it. It’s easy to defend the claim[1] that FP is exceptionally suitable for high performance in highly multithreaded environments. The author of Concurrency in .NET, says it more eloquently[2]: Real-world programs require interaction between tasks, such as exchanging information to coordinate work. This cannot be implemented without sharing data that’s accessible to all the tasks. Dealing with this shared state is the root of most problems related to parallel programming, unless the shared data is immutable or each task has its own copy. The solution is to safeguard all the code from those concurrency problems. No compiler or tool can help you position these primitive synchronization locks in the correct location in your code. It all depends on your skill as a programmer. Because of these potential problems, the programming community has cried out, and in response, libraries and frameworks have been written and introduced into mainstream object-oriented languages (such as C# and Java) to provide concurrency safeguards, which were not part of the original language design. This support is a design correction, illustrated with the presence of shared memory in imperative and object-oriented, general-purpose programming environments. Meanwhile, functional languages don’t need safeguards because the concept of FP maps well onto concurrent programming models. As you can see for yourself, there’s nothing not to like.

Question: In programming, are talented people superior to those who work hard?
Answer: Not only in programming but in every domain in life, talented people are superior, but there’s a catch: Not all hard work is of the same type, if I may use a Haskell reference. In 2014, I was assigned to teach a short class (“Psychology of Teaching”) to a group of professors who were my father’s age—most of them between 50 and 60, while I was roughly half their age. When I entered the class, several of the more opinionated professors mentioned that they had been teaching for roughly the same number of years as my age, and wondered what I could offer that they didn’t know? I told them: A person may spend n years doing the same thing without any change or improvement, whereas another spends x years where 5x = n but with a desire to improve, tinker, and research. The former has more quantitative experience, the latter more qualitative. Do you agree? They said: well, let’s see. At the end of the month, the class was a success. I had become a sort of minor celebrity and every professor wanted to take a picture with me. Most invited me to teach at their universities! (I had to decline, though, since I can’t be in two places at once :)). The point of the story is: you can work hard with a clear aim to continuously improve: in this case you achieve superiority. But if you just work hard like a drone, then all you have is experience in a narrow sense. Nobody achieves superiority (in their domain) without goal-directed, consistent, creative, and intrinsically-motivated hard work.

Question: What is the difference between complete and full binary trees?
Answer: There seems to be a lot of confusing articles online on this and many books also gloss over it. So let’s do a Savage deep dive. :) What’s a binary tree? The binary trees are a type of tree where each node has maximum two child nodes. (Hereafter we will simply refer to it as a tree.). Here, the aqua node is the root node, the pink green ones are child nodes but the yellow and violet ones are both child and leaf node. The green and yellow are left child nodes and the pink and violet are the right child nodes. Finally, as long as a new node emerges from a node, it can also be called a parent node, even if it may, itself, be a child node at first: Children of the same parent node are also called sibling nodes. What’s a full tree? A full tree is a type of tree in which each node has an even number of nodes, but the even number cannot exceed 2. So each node must have either 0 or 2 child nodes, to qualify as a full tree. Our first image is a full tree, also sometimes referred to as either a strict tree or proper tree. The pink node has 0 children, but the green node has two children. The leaf nodes each have 0 children. Clear? A complete tree? Now, imagine we have an array of numbers which we will render as a complete tree: The rule for a complete tree is: Each node must have two children, except the leaf nodes; an important point also concerns the parents of the leaf nodes (many tutorials do not mention this!) which can have either 0, 1 or 2 child nodes provided the leaf nodes are filled continuously, from the left. Let’s do this now: Note how the pink and green parent nodes are parents to the 8, 9 and 4 leaf nodes. Green is a proper (leaf child’s) parent because it has maximal number of child nodes, while pink is not. Likewise, 1 is a proper parent and must always be so. And please note, a tree can only have one root. Finally, a complete tree can have many levels as long as they follow the rule I just mentioned. Let’s do a small quiz now. Is this a full tree? Yes it is. Is it complete? Yes, also complete because the parents of the leaf nodes have 2 nodes (out of 0, 1 or 2 possibilities) and the leaf nodes (yellow, violet, blue, orange) have no nodes. The leaf nodes are called ‘leaf’ because they cannot have child nodes regardless of what kind of a tree we’re talking about. How about this? It’s not complete because the leaf node has a gap. To correct this, we should have placed the blue node as a sibling to yellow and move the orange node to the left under the pink. How about this? Also not complete because the leaf nodes are not left-most. Move the leaf nodes under green would make this a complete tree. How about this? Yes, a complete tree, because the only existing leaf node is placed to the left. Is it also a full tree? No, because full trees have even number of nodes. Here pink has even (0) nodes, while green has 1 (odd). What do you call this? ( i m a g e A ) Is it complete? (See solutions at the end of this answer). Is it full? What about i m a g e B ? I m a g e C ? I m a g e D ? I m a g e E ? Solutions A is complete. But it’s also full. B is not a full tree because the green node has only one child. You recall that in a full binary tree, every node has either 0 or 2 children. However, B is neither complete nor full. Not full because green has only one child. And not complete because there’s a cap at the yellow level. To make it complete we would have to move blue under green, and the orange to left under pink. Image C ditto suffers from a gap problem and an odd child, so not full and not complete. Image D is not full but it is complete. Image E is full but not complete. The tree discussion doesn’t stop here but I prefer to limit this answer only to the distinction between full and complete binary trees.

Question: What are the pros and cons of learning Ruby as a first programming language?
Answer: There are no cons. It’s pros all the way. Ruby was designed to make programmers happy. It has largely succeeded. Once you learn programming in Ruby first, it will become a point of reference for other languages; you’ll be able to compare them against Ruby. Does that mean Ruby is perfect? There’s no such thing as a perfect programming language. All languages have their own trade-offs (V lang claims it has solved the trade-off problem but this claim has not been verified—yet). You’ll see how Ruby is better in some respects, but also, how in some other respects, other languages outshine it. I said it’s pros all the way because it’s easier to learn: there is no friction to stop you from quickly picking the syntax and experimenting and problem-solving. With some grit, the same is true in other languages, but in Ruby, you’ll progress faster. Then why is Ruby not extremely popular? Because prog langs are like tools—although the analogy is not precisely correct. Some tools are used in some industries more often, hence the popularity. Those industries happen to be important, so these tools get used more often. With time, this creates a community, a user-base, a knowledge-base, and enough momentum to keep going even when the industry evolves and new, better tools appear. With Ruby, it was a relatively unknown tool because it was designed by a Japanese. It would have seen more adoption had it been created in the West. Further, it was only used for backend, so it’s industry usage was limited—and already competing with established giants like C#, Java, PHP etc. Even so, it held its own and carved enough space to rank 3rd most popular language for backend dev (by usage). Still, it could not compete with more versatile languages. C# is somewhat verbose and seemingly trouble-some compared to Ruby, but this difference has largely disappeared. C# is more powerful because it was supposed to compete with the powerful C++ and the popular Java (the # was known to mean ++++, to reflect C#’s ambitions). Because of languages like C#, and others that kept springing up (Scala, Swift, etc. —each of which bring a lot of their own advantages), Ruby didn’t become more popular and widespread than it could have been. There is also the matter of personal preferences. There is the curly-braces, typed-language crowd who couldn’t accept Ruby’s dynamic nature and ‘loose’ syntax, relatively slower speed. Some people like Ruby’s syntax: (I do for smaller programs and personal projects) but it may also become problematic sometimes, since Ruby has borrowed from Perl and it’s possible to write write-only code in it (code that is difficult to read). But the curly-brace, strongly-and-statically-typed, high-performance multi-industry languages are not that difficult either, you get used to them after a while, and in some of them, types need not be specified explicitly if you don’t feel like it (C++’s auto (after C++11), Java 10’s and modern C#’s var, infer data type, while Scala, Swift, Kotlin, Typescript, Elm, F#, Haskell can directly infer). You could start with one of these, too, and make roughly similar progress—in particular, with Swift and C# because when you reach advanced levels in these two, the languages offer unique perspectives and very different experience than found in other curly-braces languages. However, I still think Ruby is a good starting point and an excellent language to think in. Programming is difficult, but Ruby makes it easier enough so you can actually become curious to try other languages and more difficult programming tasks.

Question: Does the power of positive thinking actually work? If yes, how and why?
Answer: Selling positive thinking (PT) is charlatanism. You don’t need PT when things are going well, so by definition: You are supposed to need and use PT when things are not going well. But the problem is, when things are not going well, you can’t willingly bring your mind to experience PT. It’s the same way you can’t will yourself to sleep. I remember when I was undergoing some rough patches, as soon as I’d wake up, I’d remember my problems and none of the things I’d read about PT would help. I simply took the emotional equation out of the problem so that I could concentrate on solving the problem. Sometimes, problems cannot be solved immediately, or at all. You sort of become numb and while away till either a solution comes up, and you grab it, or doesn’t and you drift afloat at least. There’s no such thing as PT. Question: What is the lowest probability event you have personally witnessed?
Answer: A rich friend of mine (a Dubai sheikh) one day had an emergency and needed to borrow money from me. I was on campus so I went to the ATM and withdrew what he wanted to borrow, but in true ADHD style, forgot to take my card back. After I left, a few minutes later, I noticed a Northern European girl (college student, probably Nordic from the accent) running in my direction and panting. She was looking at me so I stopped to see what was going on. Then I saw my bank card in her hands! Amazing because there was a lot of money in that card and a nefarious person would have withdrawn all the money and absconded with it. I was so amazed by her integrity and kindness that I did not even know how to react. I had gone a long distance and at the time, there was nobody around the ATM kiosk; so I didn’t know how she realized the card was mine. I think she may have seen me from a distance as I was emerging out of the kiosk; and by the time she arrived at the ATM, I had spent the same time going away from it. Then, in order to not lose me, she ran all the way back to bring it to me, in consideration of no return whatsoever—just because it was the right thing to do. How probable a similar event could be? I insisted on asking for her details so I could at least thank her properly—perhaps by buying her a gift or inviting her to lunch—but she wouldn’t hear of it. When I asked for her phone number she smiled and replied that it was not necessary to repay her in any way and left despite my persuasion to stay for a while so I could get to know her (you see, such a kind person would have made an excellent wife—additionally she was beautiful and I was single [and young, maybe four or five years older than her]; alas, she left too quickly and I didn’t find it polite to insist further). PS: A lot of imbecilic comments forced me to disable comments since imbeciles think however an ATM machine works in their country, it must also be the same elsewhere. There was also an imbecile who didn’t believe this happened. I’m posting a photo of the university where this happened: The ATM kiosk is on the right side by the dark gray car, and you turn right, and go about 100 meters. You see that brick-red building up north? I was already there—a significant enough distance—when I saw her running along the mini-road that leads north. She must have seen me leave the ATM kiosk because she must have been going towards it from the left side (behind the wall by silver car). For those of you who are morbidly curious, this is BLCU: Beijing Language and Culture University. I wasn’t teaching there, but my Arab friend had friends who studied there and we’d often frequent it (the cafes were nice) in the good old days when you could enter a university campus even if you didn’t study there (2007–2012 period). I sincerely hope the excellent young lady who did me this favor somehow comes across this post some day and contacts me on Quora. :) I don’t know about now since I no longer work in China, but in that period, you would insert your ATM card into the machine, withdraw all you want, and then take your card back. If the card was inserted and you left, it wouldn’t have prompted for a password again. The young lady being a foreign student in China knew that. That’s why it’s such a big deal that she didn’t steal when she easily could have. May she have a long and happy life, wherever she is!
